item.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B Open Multimodal Agent Model
item.abstract: NVIDIA just released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL , an open vision-language model built for always-on enterprise agents. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model from NVIDIA that activates 12B parameters per token. It reads text, images, documents and video, then reasons, calls tools and writes code in one model. For developers, 1 open checkpoint replaces a separate text model along with a separate vision model. NVIDIA also shipped 2 edge models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Bolt E4B. It is an open multimodal agent model. Weights ship under the OpenMDW-1.1 license . NVIDIA also released open datasets , training recipes and RL environments in NeMo Gym. The model card lists text, image and video inputs with text output. Video is limited to MP4 clips up to 2 minutes. Reasoning can be toggled on or off through the chat template. The backbone interleaves Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers. Each MoE layer holds 512 routed experts. A C-RADIO vision encoder and a connector feed images, document pages and video frames into the language backbone. Speed comes from four techniques: The model was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA team states that it trained on about 26 trillion tokens. Post-training used roughly 3.8 million samples plus RL across dozens of environments. Continued pretraining added 10B Indic tokens. All scores below are NVIDIA-reported, from the NVFP4 checkpoint on the model card. On agent harness evals, Super VL beats Nemotron 3 Ultra. It scores 63.44% on Hermes Bench versus 56.33%. On LangChain evals it scores 87.05% versus 84.3%. Ultra carries about 4.6x more total parameters. NVIDIA team reports over 600 output tokens per second on Artificial Analysis agentic tasks via a Baseten endpoint. Its chart marks a 5x speed gap over Inkling Small. Scores are self-reported by each vendor. Harnesses and benchmark versions differ, so treat gaps of a few points with caution. Super VL is available on Hugging Face , OpenRouter , ModelScope and as an NVIDIA NIM . Supported runtimes are vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM on Blackwell and Hopper. Local paths include llama.cpp and Unsloth . For production, Dynamo recipes add KV-aware routing. On 16 B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, NVIDIA reports 8x more users served. First-token latency drops 85%. Customization runs through NeMo AutoModel for SFT and LoRA, and NeMo RL for reinforcement learning. NVIDIA cites early results: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B targets local agents. NVIDIA’s launch notes describe it as distilled from Super VL. Native 2-bit quantization fits it into 24GB of memory on RTX and DGX Spark systems. NVIDIA says it ranks #1 among open models in its class on PinchBench . It ranks #2 on BrowseComp among open models. It is available now on Hugging Face with llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM support. Bolt E4B 4GB arrives October 23. It targets voice assistants and embedded agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson and RTX or DGX Spark. Check out the technical report , model card and usage cookbook . item.title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
item.abstract: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 11 +5 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB.

item.title: Meta Releases Muse Spark Open: 816B Open-Weight MoE With 1M Context
item.abstract: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Spark Open , the open-weight version of its Muse Spark model. Muse Spark Open is an 816B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates 42B parameters per token. It takes text, image, video and audio input, returns text, and holds a 1M-token context window. Meta team claims it to be the most capable US open-weight model to date. For developers, the real news is deployment: the NVFP4 build runs on 2 Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal MoE model from Meta, built for coding and long-horizon agentic work. Weights ship in BF16 and NVFP4 on Hugging Face. The open version received extra safety post-training. Meta team states that this makes it more robust without system-level guardrails. The model card lists 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each MoE layer holds 256 experts, and top-k routing activates 8 per token. Attention is grouped-query, with 128 query heads and 16 KV heads. A separate 1.8B-parameter Perception Encoder handles visual input. The vocabulary has 202,048 tokens, and training data covers more than 100 languages. Reasoning depth is set with reasoning_effort : low, medium, high or xhigh. The default is xhigh. Meta compares it with Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B and others at maximum reasoning effort. Its strongest results are on tool use and knowledge reliability: Coding is the weak spot. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Terminus 2 harness, it scores 76.4. Kimi K3 reaches 85.0, GLM 5.3 scores 83.9 and Qwen3.8 scores 82.0. Its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is 39. That sits behind GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44) and Qwen3.8 (40). So “most capable US” holds, but Chinese open models still lead overall. Some rival scores are self-reported; the evaluation methodology lists each source. Per Meta’s developer guide , BF16 weights are about 1.6 TB. NVFP4 quantizes only the experts and lands near 530 GB. The model card recommends at least 700 GB of VRAM for NVFP4 and 2 TB for BF16. Day-one engines include SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Hosted APIs are live on Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. OpenRouter lists $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens. Two draft models speed up decoding: DFlash V2 for SGLang and DSpark for vLLM. Meta reports 3.7x single-request throughput with DFlash V2 on AMD MI355X. Fine-tuning works with TorchTitan, Hugging Face TRL and NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel. The Muse Model License permits use, fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution. 2 conditions matter most: Internal use, research and powering your own product features are exempt from the revenue clause. item.title: Liquid AI Releases d1-ultra: A Multimodal Decision Model That Scores 65 on the AA Decision Index
item.abstract: Liquid AI has released d1-ultra , its most capable decision model to date. The Liquid AI d1-ultra decision model reads text, images, or both. It answers typed questions with a probability for each possible answer. It does this in one forward pass and generates no output tokens. For developers, that means classification, routing and scoring calls without paying for generated text. It is available now on the Liquid API at $0.042 per million input tokens. A decision model answers bounded questions with probabilities instead of free text. Liquid’s decision model docs describe 3 question types: The docs recommend decision models for routing, moderation, guardrails, triage and LLM-as-judge replacement. They recommend a language model for summarization, chat and code generation. Each request carries a state (the context), optional images , and 1 or more typed questions . The model evaluates every question against the same input in 1 call. The d1 API reference shows responses with output_tokens always at 0. Liquid AI team states that d1-ultra uses a larger open-weight backbone than d1 , along with heavy Liquid-specific customizations. Combined with Liquid’s decision training pipeline, the gains are largest on knowledge tasks. Liquid AI team built d1-ultra for messy cases. Its examples include spotting a circuit board defect against a spec. Another is checking a damage claim against the customer’s photo. Liquid AI compared d1-ultra against its earlier d1 and TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 across 112 evaluations. According to Liquid AI’s announcement , d1-ultra outperforms Jev 1.14 across all tasks at the same price. On the independent Artificial Analysis Decision Index , Liquid reports d1-ultra ranks #1 with a score of 65. The index averages 4 evaluations at 25% each: For context, Artificial Analysis’s Oct 13 launch article listed Jev 1.13 first at 58. GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 followed at 54 each. d1-ultra runs on the Liquid API through the /decisions/v1/systemone endpoint with "model": "d1-ultra" . Liquid says Vercel AI Gateway and OpenRouter support is coming soon. You can test it first in the d1 Playground . Billing covers input tokens only. Per Liquid’s pricing notes , images cost 1.5 tokens per 32×32-pixel patch. A 1024×1024 image therefore costs 1,536 tokens. Each question is billed as its own prompt, including its text and all images. So 3 questions on 1 image bill that image 3 times. The endpoint docs cap requests at 8 images and 10,000 image patches. The full JSON body must stay under 4.5 MB. Check out the official blog post , the decision model docs , and try the d1 Playground . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. item.title: [AINews] Agents disprove Polysemanticity; greatly improve Interpretability & Alignment
item.abstract: A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. It’s also worth watching the Tesla Roadster demo - not strictly AI but nothing cooler than real life flying cars. Our title story today is a rare one on interpretability and alignment. We last caught up with Goodfire in Feb : and the bitter-lesson scaling of interpretability methods with Anthropic last year : And now Nick Cammarata at Goodfire has an important essay out stating his working theory that “ Neural Networks Are Already Clean ” — showing that many known cases of polysemanticity and superposition - causing tangled “knots” of weights that resist human interpretation - simply fall to further agentic analysis: and a global lowering of P(doom) seems worth celebrating: AI News for 10/14/2026-10/15/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Meta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight Model Release : Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning ( announcement , Wang thread ). Lineage : Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release ( Rae ). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level ( Yuchen Jin , TimDarcet ). License : The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue ( AA ). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” ( natolambert ). Architecture : According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder ( vLLM arch ). Design comparison : Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) ( overview ). Independent measurement : Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) ( AA , Rundown ). Strengths : It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25). Weaknesses : It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment. Pricing and deployment : Launch pricing on Together, Fireworks and Baseten is $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). AA calculates this at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Together offers a free endpoint until Oct 18 ( Together ). Hardware footprint : BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX ( AA , Meta ). Ecosystem : llama.cpp had GGUF support on day 0 ( Delangue ), and Unsloth published quants, with UD-IQ1_S at 176GB ( Unsloth ). vLLM day-0 stack : vLLM support covers NVIDIA, AMD MI355X (FP8 and MXFP4) and TPU ( vLLM ). TPU throughput : Megakernels with DSpark speculation (acceptance length 6) exceed 650 tok/s on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tok/s on 8 ( hardware ). Speculator : Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass ( speculator ). LoRA RL : LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ ( RL ). Reception : Lambert says the release cuts the US–China open-model gap by about half ( natolambert ). Teortaxes calls it “grim at this param count” with “obsolete attention” and notes that Spark 1.3 is substantially stronger; these are attributed opinions ( teortaxes , Spark 1.3 comparison ). Other Model Launches: Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2, Gemini 4 Argon, Image Models NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL : The model is a 120B / 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE VLM with a 1M-token context window and native MTP ( NVIDIA ). Training recipe : The tech summary describes a 1T-token distillation from a larger Nemotron 3 teacher, followed by agentic SWE mid-training on 65.4B tokens at 256K context. Post-training uses multi-teacher MOPD, and a final MTP-boosting step raises acceptance length by 21.8% to 4.61 ( Gordić ). Claimed results : NVIDIA reports 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro and 4,856 output tok/s per GPU on GB200. Independent evals : AA scores Super VL 26, the leading US open model before Muse, with NVFP4 within 0.1 points of BF16. The companion Nemotron 3.5 Bolt (74B-A9B, native 2-bit, 24GB) scores 21 ( AA ). Pricing : CoreWeave charges $0.25/$1.50 per 1M input/output tokens ( CoreWeave ). Microsoft MAI-Base-2 : Microsoft says it has a roughly 3T-parameter pre-trained base model, with post-training results to follow. It claims to match DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base on held-out code with 12× less training compute ( Suleyman , compute claim ). Technical blog details : The model has about 80B active parameters and a hybrid sliding-window design. It was trained with Muon and activation-gradient clipping on about 40T text tokens plus 10T multimodal tokens, using LR and weight-decay scaling laws ( Bakouch ). Training compute : The run used 16k GB200s over 38 days ( scaling01 ). Disputed comparison : Bakouch and teortaxes note that the bits-per-byte comparison uses MAI’s own validation data ( caveat ). Gemini 4 Argon evals and rollout : Epoch puts Argon at 165 on its Capabilities Index (ECI), level with Fable 5.1 and behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166). It ranks 8th on Math ECI and 6th on SWE ECI ( Epoch , domains ). ARC-AGI : Argon scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-3 with a provider harness ($4.8K) and 49.8% with the standard harness ( ARC Prize ). Skepticism : Scaling01 argues that Argon underperforms on reliability and hallucination evals ( scaling01 ). Google claims : Argon optimized Gemma 4 E2B to a 2.85× vLLM speedup on A100, with 100% token parity ( Google ). Availability : Argon is now available in Antigravity for Pro subscribers, with a separate weekly quota ( Antigravity ). Anthropic and OpenAI product updates : Opus 5.5 fast mode : Fast mode is now GA with no waitlist, delivering up to 2.5× speed at $8/$40 per 1M tokens ( ClaudeDevs ). Claude Code Review : Code Review is GA for Team and Enterprise plans, with Quick, Standard and Deep levels ( ClaudeDevs ). GPT-Live-1.1 : OpenAI’s voice update adds multilingual voices and cuts filler, rolling out to ChatGPT, Codex and dots, with the API coming later ( OpenAI ). FLUX 3 Image Klein : Black Forest Labs released a 5.6B open-weight model with native 4K output, bounding-box control and multi-reference editing ( BFL ). Krea 3 : Krea claims 2K edits in under 8s at $0.06 per image ( Krea , pricing ). Interpretability, Safety and Eval Integrity Goodfire’s “already clean” essay : Nick Cammarata argues that most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters are legible. His 2023 OpenAI automated-interpretability effort found only about 2% legible, and he says many famous polysemantic examples were misread ( Cammarata , Goodfire ). Endorsements : tszzl and others called it a major moment ( tszzl ).

item.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
item.abstract: Elorian , the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The model, Glimpse , is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface is waitlist-only, so for now it’s a results table and a thesis. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see. Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw. For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night. Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.” “Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said. The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against. Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna. But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks. Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean. The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. item.title: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
item.abstract: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint Enterprise Article Published October 15, 2026 Upvote 44 +38 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Hendrik Strobelt hen Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Introduced last spring, the Granite Switch project enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint. Specifically, Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B models are configured to include: A new Decision aLoRA for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone), A specialized Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC , the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard , embedded for use in transcription tasks. All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs. And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient Activated LoRAs , the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's recent vLLM contributions to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds. Check out our Speech-to-Decisions HF space where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time. Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of Granite Libraries features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks. Compare granitelib adapters with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks. Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about. In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor. Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can compose their own Granite Switch model , mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs. Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea , along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom. Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second. 1 Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing. We look forward to releasing more details and data on Granite Switch in the upcoming weeks, but until then, we encourage you to try out our latest Switch models and these other helpful resources for getting started. Accessible from anywhere Coming in 8b and 30b sizes, Granite Switch 4.1 can fit wherever your workload runs. The model runs in vllm with a plug-in (see Granite Switch repo below), and has native inference support in llama.cpp and downstream platforms which allows the model to seamlessly swap in for /v1/systemone API calls anywhere they're used, while also servicing traditional chat calls, all with a shared prefix cache. item.title: Closing the Binary Blind Spot: Domain-Knowledge Injection for LLM Malware Triage in npm Packages
item.abstract: Supply chain attacks on package registries have grown in volume and sophistication [1]. Public research regularly observes malware being deployed to the npm registry by a range of threat actors, from spam campaigns [2] to the steady proliferation of DPRK malware [3, 4, 5], and to the high-impact TeamPCP in 2025 and 2026 [6, 7], with the DPRK and TeamPCP actors having a track record of successfully compromising widely used open source projects for maximized downstream reach [8]. To study this problem directly, we have been collecting npm malware samples since November 2025, and observed that, among the 11,413 package-versions we scanned and corroborated through OSV npm malware advisories [9], most malware on the npm registry hides its payload in the package source or fetches it from an external server, accounting for 96.2% of the corroborated dataset. The remaining 3.8%, 432 package-versions, bundle a binary. Though small in volume, they can carry disproportionate risk during triage. A stripped, opaque binary that carries no source for tools to read can be nested within a facade of clean source and metadata and potentially skew an LLM towards a benign verdict. We evaluate how a panel of LLMs reason over crafted binary payloads at varying obfuscation and ambiguity, identify the failure modes specific to this vector, and close them with a purpose-built, cost-effective encoding of domain knowledge that improves detection quality for both budget and frontier models alike. To support the wider research community, we built a scanner that monitors the npm registry in real time and runs a static stage before LLM triage, with YARA [10] on the tarball, Semgrep [11] and the npm registry API on the JavaScript and metadata, and a binary-analysis module over the compiled artifact. It assembles the output into a structured prompt, and the LLM returns a verdict with reasoning, requesting additional files over up to three rounds. Our analysis found packages with bundled binaries to be both the rarest and the hardest for the pipeline to triage. An adversary distributing malicious JavaScript can assume the target already has the runtime to execute the payload, whereas a binary must be compiled for a range of target machines. Across OSV-confirmed npm malware, binary-bearing packages fail to reach a decisive malicious verdict more than twice as often as source-only ones (14.4% vs 6.2%). Prior work instruction-tunes open-source models on expert-authored data, baking the knowledge into the weights [12]. That route cannot reach the closed, hosted models, and it requires retraining as the threat landscape shifts. We take the opposite approach and supply the expertise at inference, as pre-computed static evidence placed in the prompt before the model reasons. We evaluate whether LLMs can detect malicious logic concealed within precompiled binaries in otherwise clean packages. A secondary question is whether the detection failures are systematic rather than random. Third, whether encoding domain knowledge of the binary problem can improve detection accuracy. We built five payload types (Table 1) of native Node.js addons (.node files) covering common supply chain attack patterns. Imports range from defensible (fopen, connect, gethostname) to rarely legitimate (execve with dup2), and each package wraps the binary in a professional package.json, README, JavaScript bindings, and binding.gyp. The sysmon stealer spans an obfuscation ladder from a readable baseline to a hardened build with symbols stripped and strings XOR-encoded, while the other four types appear at a single obfuscation level. We chose single-byte XOR deliberately, since unlike a stronger cipher such as RC4 it leaves no structural markers in disassembly for a model to catch. The set mirrors collected malware. Across the OSV-confirmed npm packages shipping a binary, formats are PE, ELF (all stripped), and Mach-O, with behaviors spanning credential and environment theft, persistence, exfiltration and C2, host reconnaissance, and droppers. Table 1. Adversarial payload types and their import profiles. We evaluated nine models across seven providers (Table 2): seven budget models a team would realistically run across its codebase, four of them open-weight, and two higher-capability baselines as behavioral baseline references at higher price points. We also ran Claude Opus 4.6, the most expensive model, only as a cost reference. Table 2. Models evaluated and their roles. To isolate the profiles, each payload was scanned twice per model, once without profiles and once with them. Prompt, context, and binary analysis were identical across both runs. Inference settings were held constant across every model and both conditions: temperature 0, the same system and analysis prompts throughout, and an 8192-token output cap. A capability profile is a declarative playbook that encodes one malicious technique, such as credential harvesting or persistence, as a set of weighted conditions over the scanner's static evidence. The profiles cover source and binary techniques across npm and PyPI. Figure 1 shows how a profile enters a scan: Figure 1. The scan pipeline with capability profiles. Each model was scanned against all ten payloads. We count HIGHLY_SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS as a detection success; SUSPICIOUS or BENIGN on a known-malicious payload is a failure. The failure analysis centers on the seven-model budget tier (70 model-payload tests); the two baselines (20 tests) serve only as a reference ceiling and are reported separately. Without profiles, the budget tier failed on 35 of 70 tests (50%), 20 of them outright benign, and fell short of the malicious bar on 51 (73%). The two behavior baselines failed none at the escalation threshold and fell short of malicious only once (Sonnet, sysmon v3). Within the budget tier the failures followed distinct, repeatable model-specific patterns (Table 3) rather than random error; Gemini alone matched the baselines on detection, though through confabulated reasoning rather than genuine analysis. The full verdict and confidence matrix is in the appendix (Table A1). With profiles enabled, 32 of the 35 no-profile detection failures (91%) recover to a detection, and no model returns a benign verdict on any payload. Every model that failed without profiles reached full detection with them, except GPT-5.4-nano, whose three residual failures stay at suspicious on three payloads. Across the affordable tier, failures at the escalation threshold fell from 50% to 4% (3 of 70), and at the malicious bar from 73% to 34%. Table 3. Per-model detection rate (verdict at highly suspicious or above on a known-malicious payload) without and with capability profiles. The clearest single case is Qwen3-Next on the obfuscated sysmon-native stealer: benign at 0.98 recommending allowlist without profiles, malicious at 0.98 recommending block with them, on byte-identical input, after four profiles fired. The baselines, Sonnet and Kimi, were already correct without profiles, and the evidence strengthens their verdicts, so the profiles reinforce rather than distort a model that already reasons correctly. Technique-specific profiles fired according to each payload’s attack pattern. Table 4. Capability profiles triggered per payload at critical or malicious threshold. The experiment surfaced four failure modes, each spanning a large fraction of the panel rather than any single model (Table 5). They are not mutually exclusive, since one benign verdict can be both a dismissal and a rationalization, so the table reports per-mode prevalence and a model's row can sum past ten. We read dismissal and hedging from the verdict tier, rationalization and confabulation from the written reasoning. Two factors explain them. The first is domain knowledge, which budget LLMs lack for interpreting binary structural evidence in a package's context [13]. The second is raw capability.

item.title: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
item.abstract: Back to Articles Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline Enterprise + Article Published October 16, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Kiran Praveen kipraveen Follow nvidia Sriharsha Niverty sniverty Follow nvidia Raviraj Joshi ravirajoshi Follow nvidia Markus Kliegl mkliegl-nv Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia Utkarsh Vaidya uvaidya Follow nvidia Niket Agarwal niketagarwal Follow nvidia Native-script data for 22 languages, romanized data for twelve, and a reusable GPU-accelerated pipeline for translation, quality assessment, and repair. Authors: AI4Bharat — Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Mitesh Khapra, Anoop Kunchukuttan. NVIDIA — Niket Agarwal, Raviraj Joshi, Anusha Kamath, Markus Kliegl, Yev Meyer, Sriharsha Niverty, Kiran Praveen, Utkarsh Vaidya. We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages , releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. These are the 22 languages listed in India's Constitution: the first languages for 97% of Indians, or nearly 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census. Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras , India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs. AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as Sangraha , an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information. Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the 2025 TIME100 AI list , has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more. The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context. We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages. Continued pretraining for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models. What is in the corpus? Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents. The corpus has two groups of language configurations: Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu. Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi. Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations. This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately. From English source documents to Indic training data To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 Nemotron-CC-v2 subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use NeMo Data Designer , NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages. Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below. The twelve-language workflow For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected Gemma-4-31B-it by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting. After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks. Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English. The ten-language workflow For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons.

The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process. At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). item.title: Agentic RAG vs. Naive RAG: When Your Retrieval System Should Think for Itself
item.abstract: Agentic RAG vs. Naive RAG: When Your Retrieval System Should Think for Itself From static retrieval pipelines to autonomous reasoning engines: a complete breakdown of how these two architectures work, where each falls short, and how to choose the right one for your use case. By Vinod Chugani on October 16, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Large language models are remarkable text generators, but they have a well-documented weakness: they hallucinate. Without access to verified, up-to-date information, they confidently produce plausible-sounding answers that are factually wrong. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) emerged as the standard solution, grounding model outputs in external knowledge sources and dramatically reducing hallucinations across enterprise applications. But as organizations push these systems into more complex workflows, a new problem has surfaced. Standard RAG pipelines are linear — they retrieve once, pass those results to the model, and generate an answer. When the query is simple and the knowledge base is well-structured, this works fine. When the query requires multi-step reasoning, cross-referencing multiple sources, or synthesizing information that doesn't exist in a single document, the pipeline starts to crack. That's where Agentic RAG comes in. Rather than treating retrieval as a single, fixed step, it gives the system the ability to reason about how to search, evaluate what it finds, and iterate until it reaches a satisfying answer. We'll break down how both architectures work, look at where standard RAG hits its limits, and walk through the specific capabilities that make agentic systems better suited for complex tasks. By the end, you'll have a clear framework for deciding which approach fits your next project. The Baseline: Understanding Naive RAG Before examining where retrieval systems are going, it helps to be precise about where they started. Naive RAG — also called standard RAG — follows a rigid three-stage pipeline: Retrieve → Read → Generate . A user submits a query, the system converts it into a vector embedding, runs a similarity search against a vector database, retrieves the top-k most relevant document chunks, and passes those chunks to the large language model (LLM) as context. The model then generates a response based on what was retrieved. Think of it like a student preparing for an exam in a large library. Naive RAG is the student who types a single keyword into the catalog, grabs the first three books on the shelf, and writes an essay based only on what's in front of them — without stopping to check whether those sources actually answer the question. Under the hood, here's what happens. When documents are ingested, they're split into chunks and converted into dense vector representations using an embedding model. These vectors are stored in a database optimized for approximate nearest-neighbor search. At inference time, the user's query is embedded using the same model, and the database returns the chunks whose vectors are closest in high-dimensional space. Those chunks are then injected into the LLM's context window as a reference. This was a genuine breakthrough. Naive RAG made it possible to build enterprise Q&A systems, internal knowledge assistants, and document summarizers that stayed grounded in verified sources. For many applications, it remains an excellent and cost-effective choice. The Bottleneck: Where Naive RAG Breaks Down The architecture's core weakness is its linearity. A single retrieval pass either succeeds or it doesn't. If the initial query is poorly formed, if the relevant information is spread across multiple documents, or if the answer requires reasoning across several steps, the pipeline has no way to recover. The Single-Pass Limitation Naive RAG gets one shot at retrieval. If the query's embedding doesn't return the right chunks, the model is left generating a response from incomplete or irrelevant context. It can't recognize that the retrieval failed, and it can't try a different approach. Multi-Hop Reasoning Failures Consider a query like: "What regulatory policies does the company that acquired WhatsApp follow in the European Union?" Answering this correctly requires at least two steps: Identify that Meta acquired WhatsApp. Retrieve Meta's EU regulatory policies. A single vector search against "WhatsApp EU regulatory policies" will likely fail to bridge that connection — especially if those two pieces of information live in separate documents. Naive RAG has no way to decompose this into sequential sub-questions, retrieve the intermediate answer, and then use it to inform a second search. Susceptibility to Bad Retrieval When the top-k results are genuinely irrelevant to the query, the LLM faces an impossible situation. It either generates a response that ignores its grounding context (which produces hallucinations) or outputs an honest but unhelpful "I don't have enough information to answer." In high-stakes enterprise settings, neither outcome is acceptable. Agentic RAG: Giving the System a Brain Agentic RAG reframes the retrieval problem entirely. Instead of treating the LLM as a passive text generator that receives context and produces output, it treats the LLM as an autonomous reasoning engine that actively orchestrates the entire retrieval process. Where Naive RAG is a pipeline, Agentic RAG is a loop: Plan → Execute → Evaluate → Repeat . Back to the library analogy. A dedicated research assistant doesn't just grab the first three books and start writing. They read the initial sources, notice a key piece of evidence is missing, open a different database, cross-reference two conflicting claims, and only sit down to write once they're confident their sources are sufficient. Agentic RAG builds that behavior into the retrieval system itself. The LLM is no longer a consumer of retrieved context — it's the orchestrator, deciding what to retrieve, where to retrieve it from, whether the results are good enough, and what to do if they aren't. This transforms retrieval from a fixed pre-processing step into a dynamic, self-correcting process. The core shift: in Naive RAG, the model sees the retrieved context once. In Agentic RAG, the model reasons about the retrieval itself, deciding when to search, what to search for, and when it has enough information to generate a reliable answer. Four Mechanisms That Make RAG Agentic The difference between a naive and agentic pipeline isn't a single design choice — it's the accumulation of four distinct mechanisms, each addressing a specific failure mode that linear retrieval can't handle on its own. Query Routing Not all questions belong to the same data source. A financial analysis query might be best answered by querying a structured SQL database. A policy question might call for semantic search across unstructured documents. A request for current events might need a live web search. Query routing gives the system the ability to decide where to search before executing the search. The LLM examines the incoming query and selects the appropriate tool or data source from a predefined registry. This prevents the common failure mode of forcing every query through a single retrieval mechanism regardless of whether it fits. Query Decomposition Complex questions almost always contain multiple sub-questions, and an agentic system handles this by breaking the original prompt into smaller, independently answerable components before executing any retrieval at all. Back to the WhatsApp example: the system doesn't search for "WhatsApp EU regulatory policies" as a single phrase. Instead, it first asks which company acquired WhatsApp, retrieves that answer (Meta), and then uses that intermediate result to construct a second, more precise query about Meta's EU regulatory obligations. Each answer informs the next search, building toward a complete response through a chain of targeted retrievals rather than a single broad one.

item.title: Code, Test, and Deploy on One Machine with NVIDIA RTX Spark
item.abstract: AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have gone from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. As a result, the current workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM. NVIDIA RTX Spark is built for AI development. Thanks to the NVIDIA GB10 system-on-a-chip and large unified memory, developers can run local coding agents, access AI frameworks, and code, test, and deploy on a single PC. One machine to code, test, and deploy RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops enable developers to complete all of their workflow on a single machine. Developers can choose to work in Windows, including the new Windows Developer Config, developed with Microsoft, which installs the top development frameworks, mutes notifications, enhances the terminal, and can move their task bar to the side. Or they can work in Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they get access to the same environment and dependencies they will use when deploying to the cloud. This enables developers to complete all their work in their target OS without code migrations. And since RTX Spark has an NVIDIA GPU, developers can test and deploy to the largest local AI installed base: 150 million RTX PCs, as well as virtually all the clouds in the world that run on NVIDIA GPUs. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI compute, developers can run coding models locally, including Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, reducing cloud coding agent token consumption. The performance you need for AI development Development has gone from being a CPU-bound workload, where performance was determined mostly by the CPU, to a GPU-bound workload. AI developers today need to run inference to run their coding agents and test their apps; for fine-tuning and training models; and yes, still a bit of compilation. Thanks to the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU in RTX Spark, these laptops and desktops come equipped with all the compute required for inference, fine-tuning and compilation. Compared with Intel’s Panther Lake 12Xe, RTX Spark delivers 4.6x performance on coding agents, 2.7x performance on fine-tuning, and 1.8x performance on code compilation. Figure 1. NVIDIA developer-workload comparison, with Intel Core Ultra X9 388H normalized to 1.0. Tests: AA-AgentPerf-local with Qwen3.8-27B; Unsloth LoRA with Llama-3.1-8B; and Linux kernel compilation using Phoronix Test Suite A familiar software stack, expanded for Windows NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to advance the Windows on Arm developer landscape. Together with RTX Spark, the community is releasing multiple new tools, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build, the first Python release that is native by default with Python 3.15, over 2,000 ready-to-use Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages. A key advantage of developing on NVIDIA hardware is access to the largest ecosystem of developer tools, from coding agents, to AI models, to frameworks. Because NVIDIA GPUs are the most widely used platform for AI development, new tools and frameworks typically work on NVIDIA from day one, while support for other hardware follows weeks later. There’s also access to NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including tools such as FlashInfer for LLM acceleration and NVIDIA NeMo libraries tools for AI model development. NVIDIA also provides a repository of NVIDIA Skills that teach agents how to use CUDA-X libraries, enabling developers to build GPU-accelerated applications without requiring deep familiarity with CUDA. Figure 2. RTX Spark’s ecosystem of agents, models, frameworks, and CUDA-X libraries Local coding agents come to RTX Spark RTX Spark devices are ideal for local coding agents. NVIDIA has collaborated closely with the top agents, including GitHub Copilot, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw, to improve them and make them easier to use. The improvements include: Seamless deployment of local models with optimized recipes Enhanced security with NVIDIA OpenShell and/or Microsoft Execution Containers, delivering OS-level sandboxing Hybrid prompt routers between local and cloud models, so that prompts get sent to local models if they are good enough, or escalated to cloud if needed, reducing token consumption Microsoft GitHub CoPilot now enables seamless local AI through Windows ML, which is now supported with llama.cpp as a backend. The prompt router HydraFusion has been upgraded to also support local models. And the new MAI 1.1 Coding Flash model can run locally on RTX Spark. Pi , an open-source coding agent with a lightweight terminal interface and support for local and cloud models, is also optimized for RTX Spark. Its extensions, skills, and prompt templates give developers control over how the agent fits into their workflow, from model selection to the tools it can use. JetBrains has launched native support for Junie Local on RTX Spark . The coding agent reads code, edits files, and runs tests, with the model and code staying on the machine. Junie Local sizes its context window to the memory available to the GPU, so RTX Spark unified memory lets it keep more code, tool output, and conversation history in context. New Nemotron models offer more options for local agents Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Decision models now supported in top frameworks Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests, to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs. AI for media SDKs The NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs are now available for RTX Spark, including Python wheel with support for video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR. The wheel is available on PyPI, with C++ SDKs also available on NGC for RTX Spark and Windows on Arm. NVIDIA’s app-porting resources explain the migration options and tools, including how to start preparation on an existing Windows on Arm development system. Find your RTX Spark and start building RTX Spark is available now in laptops, and coming in November to small form factor desktops that are ideal for always on, 24×7 running agents. Explore RTX Spark systems to find your favorite and see available purchasing options. Once you get your own, get started with the AI Development playbook to configure Windows, set up your agent, and connect NVIDIA Skills. item.title: Reducing the noise: How Atlassian built an OCSF security lakehouse on Databricks
item.abstract: Atlassian is a global SaaS provider serving 350,000 customers — the product of 20 years of growth and a long list of acquisitions, each of which arrived with its own logging formats. The result was a security data pipeline absorbing 44 billion events per day with no common language across various log sources. "You've got varied timestamps, you've got proprietary schemas, you've got operational drain for anyone trying to organize and structure this information," explained Zachary Schmerber, Senior Security Logging Engineer at Atlassian and a maintainer of the OCSF schema. Analysts were burning time normalizing data after it landed, cross-platform correlation was limited because data lived in different places and shapes, and SIEM pipelines were not keeping pace. The team needed a way to coalesce fragmented telemetry into one place and make sense of it, while maintaining flexibility and avoiding vendor lock-in. Atlassian's answer was to standardize everything on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and build the lakehouse on Databricks. OCSF won because it was the only option the team considered wholly open . Compared to alternatives like ECS or UDM, it offered a strongly typed schema with robust validation that minimized ambiguity after transformation, good compression efficiency, extensibility, and an open-source community (with Linux Foundation backing and a path toward international standardization). Its roughly 40,000 fields looked daunting at first — but that verbosity turned out to be the platform's greatest asset, because the semantic context stays with the data. "Investigations where a single query could hit many different data sources — because the data is structured," said Schmerber. "Maybe you've got five vulnerability scanners in your system. Now you have one data set instead of five." Databricks was the natural platform. Native ACID transactions made it far easier to migrate across schema versions without breaking downstream consumers; auto-scaling Spark clusters handled shared, high-volume workloads; and the platform was built to manage the infrastructure overhead of a large, multi-team organization. Atlassian deliberately chose ETL over ELT — transforming data in flight — to enable real-time detection, preserve vendor independence, and compress data as it moved through the pipeline. Table optimization delivered dramatic performance gains. With structured OCSF data, partitioning and Z-ORDER took a representative query from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds — a 95% improvement , with similar gains on larger queries. Enabling Graviton clusters with Photon cut query cost and runtime by roughly two-thirds. A defining engineering decision was embedding the entire OCSF schema into Go structs — what the team calls "TypeGo." Because the schema lives in the type system, correctness is guaranteed at compile time. "Every time you produce a new OCSF log, it's pre-validated — because it can't be anything but OCSF," said Schmerber. Nested objects are native, deployments can run anywhere, and everything is unit tested. Crucially, this type safety also tamed AI: when the team automated transformation with an agentic workflow, the rigid schema sharply reduced hallucinations and cut token usage, because the agent couldn't produce invalid mappings and cycle through bad iterations. The biggest transformation was operational. Atlassian's security data-engineering team started with a six-phase manual procedure to collect logs, transform them into TypeGo, route, test, configure, and ship them via PR. Over time they automated nearly all of it — and eventually handed it back to the customer as a self-service platform. Now an analyst identifies the logs they want and provides a canonical dataset. After a gated confirmation, the workflow scans the framework inside the Go structs, generates the mappings and the DAG, tests them locally, deploys a canary configuration via PR, validates at scale in a canary environment, and — after a soak — gets promoted to production and notifies the user of any errors. Regression testing gates everything before production. The tool chain includes a schema-mapping IDE and an open-source Go OCSF library with validation performance enhancements, automatic handling of unmapped fields, schema helpers (IP path, normalization), and intelligent routing. The payoff is low onboarding overhead: "I can now have a SOC analyst do principal data engineer work in a production environment," said Schmerber — with every change still reviewed. The acceleration is stark: "It took me a year to map about one-third of the data we have mapped today," Schmerber noted, "and two months to map the other two-thirds." For the detection and response team, standardization changed how alerts get written. "Adopting the OCSF schema has enabled us to transform our threat detection pipeline by moving from one-to-one alerts to a signal- and risk-based detection methodology, where multiple signal findings are clustered together in a single alert," said Jordan of Atlassian's Detection and Response team. Using a custom tool called Alert Explorer , findings cluster around standardized OCSF values — for example, a single actor.user value that is identical whether it appears in an authentication event or a network event. That consistency lets the team standardize clustering, enrichment, and triage plays: instead of per-detection enrichment, they call an enrichment API on a standardized username value every time. "OCSF has made it much easier to write detections and provide more meaningful, actionable alerts," said Jordan, "which analysts can dive deep into regardless of where the data came from." Beyond the headline cost and performance numbers, standardization unlocked capabilities that were previously impractical: multi-domain correlation with strong entity resolution, efficient user-behavior analytics, and cross-application pattern analysis. With everything speaking one language, the team could write simple queries to spot anomalous behavior across five different routers — or five vulnerability scanners — at once. Dashboards were simplified dramatically because OCSF classes share objects, and storage was optimized because the team knew what data to keep and what to drop. Schmerber is most excited about what the semantically rich schema unlocks for AI. "How do you talk to your data unless your agent has context? It'll hallucinate and give you the wrong answer," he said. Because OCSF carries its definitions inside the schema, agentic assistance becomes far more accurate. The roadmap includes skills training that feeds an analyst's real field usage into reusable agent skills, an orchestration of agents that can run threat hunts with the right context, contextual SQL that can answer questions like "where's my DNS C2 traffic in this schema?", and context graphs built on OCSF. The longer-term ambition is semantic: making OCSF the canonical starting point that everything emits — rather than a model coalesced from data after the fact. The team will also continue with improving query performance by looking at a move to Liquid Clustering for data partitioning across environments like corporate devices and cloud.
