item.title: AI #190: Scion of the Times
item.abstract: The amount of code being written at Anthropic continues to rise exponentially. It is being managed by Scion, their internal replacement for GitHub that is better suited to the scale and style of the operation, which they created with a small team in five months. This week also saw the release of two supposed frontier model models. Google has finally given us Gemini 4 Argon, along with a robust safety report. We do not yet know if Argon lives up to its benchmarks or internal hype. I plan to write up the safety report next week, time permitting. If and only if it is good enough or discussed enough we will also have a full report on capabilities. Meta gave us Muse Wonder, which like Argon has some excellent benchmarks, although they were presented in a way that looked rather sus. There are some reports that it is very good, but again it is too early to know. I will issue a full report if and only if Muse Wonder has capabilities or discussion that seem worthy. To help me decide and to let people have fun, I have markets on whether I will issue the reports on Argon and Wonder , respectfully. OpenAI caught an employee planting a bug. How many more spies are out there? A group used ChatGPT to create a full-chain exploit of Chrome and claimed a $250,000 bounty. Luckily for us it was the good guys this time. Like most weeks, I covered a lot more. It was only a little over a week ago that OpenAI dumped solutions to hundreds of math problems . Then came news that OpenAI fired three safety researchers , without providing us a good explanation. Once again we went over the fact that arguments about AI consciousness remain highly motivated and at best overconfident . Finally, I emphasized that the safety culture at the labs is broken , which is one of the most important facts about the world. Today I am flying out to another conference at Lighthaven. I probably posted this from the airport and it won’t include any events from last night, tomorrow’s post will be the monthly and Monday may be from the non-AI queue. This coming week will then be another case of me scrambling to catch up, especially with the model reviews still potentially looming. Prompting is easy now. As Boris Cherny says, tell the AI what you want to do , how to verify that it did it, and how much effort to spend, and you’re good. I’d add ‘and anything it needs to know.’ Presumably that was implied. Boris prompts on Slack , which means Claude already has a lot of context, enabling shorter prompts. Do you trust Grok to go use your credit card without pausing for approval? Elon Musk : To buy stuff, you can just take a picture of your credit card, drop it in the chat and Grok @Bot will scour the Internet for the best deal on the item you want and order it. [Community note: No that’s not how you upload your CC information.] The correct maximally allowed error rate on such actions is not zero. It also is not high, and if you are using this blind you likely will have no idea if it is getting the best price or the best item. Then again, did you know before? How easy is prompting? Pliny shuffled this off to Opus 5.5 with a $200 subscription: “can you wraite a promtp for a cron job that can run every day thajt will try to find solutions to unsolved ciphers or transltions or math problems or theormes or things of that nature!! every day a new attempt as hard as possible all day without giving ujp and with maximum ceraitvityy, resourcesleflses, andpersticense! dont worry about token spend! and dont forget a bit all caps lots of emojis celebration to notify the uers if we get any intersting or sucsfful confirmd reulsts!!”​ day 1, the legion picked its own target: J.-F. Bouchaudy’s cipher-machine challenges. these are simulations of real vintage machines (Hebern rotor machines, the Kryha, Lorenz, SIGABA), with problems that had been sitting on his solver tables with no solver for months or years. on the morning of day 2, i was half asleep when my laptop suddenly says, in a robot voice: “Breakthrough. The Daily Oracle has a confirmed solution.” then the ALL CAPS emoji flood hits my screen. Hebern 5-rotor Problem 8 then Kryha v2 Problem 5 i emailed the author, Jean-François Bouchaudy, a French cryptography enthusiast who builds these machine simulators and challenges as a labor of love (he told me he started out programming on punch cards ). he checked both solutions and put my name on his solver tables as the first and only solver This is the correct version of ‘do a breakthrough, make no mistakes.’ It’s that easy. A thought experiment from Terence Tao : It seems ethical, in a sane world, to allow volunteers to participate in such trials. If the cocktail passes a Phase 3 trial, then we should conclude that it works. No, I absolutely would not, if I had cancer, demand that there was a human who ‘understood how it works,’ and if the FDA required that I would yell about it a lot. Yes, of course you would also want to model tail risks that might not be showing up and take those risks into account, so I wouldn’t use this lightly, but if the cancer is lethal and otherwise untreatable then why not? Obviously you would also have to worry about some form of active misalignment, and that this was part of some sort of takeover or similar attempt, at that point, but that is a very different concern than the ones Tao is presumably considering. Tao instead has the next point be ‘the AI hacked the FDA and the drug both does not work and kills people’ but even if the AI is being malicious for the lulz no one going to do this by hacking the FDA, in the sense that the Phase 3 trial is a physical thing with many artifacts in the world, that is then examined by humans? So we would just notice. And if we didn’t, we’d notice pretty quickly after that. The only real risk is long-latency-only harm, which is already true today and has limited downside if you are treating otherwise deadly cancers. Talk and write to people whose expertise lies elsewhere: Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): By the way, in my experience contractors of all sorts have adopted AI for text-based communications and it has substantially improved coordination on home renovation projects Remember that, no matter how great Opus 5.5 is (and it’s pretty great), how many contributions you make or lines of code you write is not a good measure of productivity. Ado (Anthropic): The weekend after Opus 5.5 launched I had my most productive coding day of the year (so far). AI writing now once again lags behind AI math. Matthew Yglesias : AI cracking unsolvable math problems while being kinda mid at writing is a much-needed W for humanities majors after a rough 21st century. Paul Graham : Apparently it’s mostly just because they haven’t made much of an effort to train it to write well yet. Matthew Yglesias : I’ve been reliably informed my work isn’t economically valuable enough to be worth investing time on automating. Miles Brundage : Mostly just cuz there are like 2 ppl working on it though Matthew Yglesias : Let us have this Better AI writing would be highly economically valuable, so my guess is this is mostly not ‘we forgot to put 10 or even 50 guys on it instead of 2.’ You’d have to work a lot harder than that. The alternative hypothesis is ‘you may not like it but this is what peak performance looks like,’ that the people love their Claudeslop and it works, and we would react inherently negatively to AI writing no matter what it sounds like. Sure, it would be better if for those who care it could vary more and be higher Quality, but is that worth the price? I don’t know. I can see it both ways. My guess is the Claudeslop has short term benefits, but continued use of it accumulates long term costs and fatigue. In general, when faced with such choices, modern capitalism is often myopic and gets in trouble. Who gets the blame if AI fails ? Opinions differ greatly. It depends on the situation. There is no universal answer. Meta’s Muse Wonder exists .

item.title: How our AI Research team uses AI Runtime
item.abstract: At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to make our products more intelligent, efficient, and useful for customers. Our research spans products like Genie, Smart Routing, and AI Functions. Recently, we've published how we made search 3x faster , developed new techniques for offline reinforcement learning , and pushed the frontier of complex document extraction . To build great AI models and manage hundreds of parallel research workstreams, we need infrastructure that can keep pace. That's why we use Databricks AI Runtime (AIR). In this post, we'll share how AIR helps us experiment quickly, scale to large training workloads, and adapt to agent-led training, along with what we've learned about managing GPU resources across research projects. Our research team develops models that power Databricks AI Functions , including ai_parse_document and ai_extract . For example, Databricks AI Functions deliver state-of-the-art document parsing quality , backed by models trained to understand enterprise documents. Achieving that quality requires extensive research across different architectures, datasets, training techniques, and hyperparameters, spanning tens of thousands of training and evaluation runs. We use supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline reinforcement learning (RL), and online RL to train models ranging from a few billion parameters to nearly a trillion. Depending on the workload, we use NVIDIA H100 or B300 GPUs, both available through AIR. Our largest training runs can require hundreds of GPUs working together over days or weeks, with high-bandwidth networking to keep training efficient. Supporting these workloads creates three challenges: Our research team has been customer zero of AI Runtime since the product's inception last year. We use AIR to develop, train, and test models that power Databricks AI products, relying on its GPU infrastructure and integration with our existing tools. AIR performs preflight checks on assigned GPU nodes to ensure they're healthy and can communicate effectively before training starts. It also monitors node health during execution, detecting issues such as NCCL communication failures, thermal or power throttling, and GPU driver problems. If a node becomes unhealthy and causes a job to fail, AIR detects the issue and cordons off the affected node so subsequent jobs aren't scheduled on the same problematic infrastructure. This is especially important for projects like KARL, where complex rollout generation and post-training of models with more than 100 billion parameters can require thousands of GPU hours. Rather than repeatedly troubleshooting infrastructure failures, we can focus on improving our models. Fast iteration with the AIR CLI and custom containers Research requires us to change model configurations, training approaches, and code frequently. With the AIR CLI, we can launch workloads programmatically, specify the GPUs we need, and let AIR handle provisioning and scheduling, including high-bandwidth networking for distributed training across clouds. We also rely on custom Docker containers for local development. AIR lets us use those same images for training, ensuring compatibility without recreating our environments. We can upload our codebase, execute custom code in those containers, and use Databricks Artifact Registry to register and share images across experiments. AIR's investments in launch latency and container optimization help us start training jobs in seconds, shortening feedback loops as we test new ideas. MLflow and logging for experiment tracking We use MLflow to track our research experiments. AIR automatically creates and manages MLflow experiments for our training jobs, eliminating separate configuration. We can monitor job status, stream and inspect training logs, and retrieve metrics to understand how experiments are progressing. This also gives our AI agents access to the information they need to evaluate results and determine what to try next. Seamless, governed access to research data All of our research data is stored in Unity Catalog. Through Unity Catalog FUSE mounting, AIR lets us access that data as though it were part of a local filesystem, even when working across different Databricks workspaces. This keeps our data accessible, tracked, shareable, and governed without changing how our training code interacts with files. Combined with MLflow and our Docker-based environments, it gives us a consistent workflow from local development to distributed training. Managing GPU capacity across research projects Our workloads have very different resource needs. A debugging experiment may require only a few GPUs, while a large training run might need hundreds for days or weeks. Different projects also have competing timelines and priorities. AIR's workload prioritization and preemption capabilities help us allocate resources across projects, prioritize time-sensitive experiments, and use excess capacity when it's available. For example, spare capacity can support additional exploratory experiments over a weekend without disrupting higher-priority work. Our goal is to keep GPU resources available for the experiments that matter, without requiring researchers to manually coordinate infrastructure. Popularized by Andrej Karpathy, autoresearch is changing how we develop AI models. Instead of researchers manually launching and evaluating every experiment, we're increasingly using agents to propose changes, run experiments, evaluate results, and determine what to try next. This shift has dramatically increased our experimentation volume. Across our AI Functions research workloads, the number of training jobs has grown by 8x . As agents take on more of the research process, our infrastructure needs to keep up. A slow startup or confusing configuration error might be manageable when a researcher launches a handful of experiments. When agents launch hundreds, those same issues quickly become bottlenecks. Agent-driven research requires fast job launches, programmatic interfaces, clear and actionable errors, reliable execution, and accessible training results. Our autoresearch workflow follows a continuous cycle: AIR is particularly well suited to this workflow because agents can interact with it programmatically and benefit from its fast job launches, built-in reliability, and ability to scale. Through the Databricks CLI and databricks-air-skills , our agents can launch concurrent workloads, monitor job status, retrieve MLflow metrics, and iterate based on the results. This lets us run more experiments while our researchers focus on developing new ideas and improving model quality. As we move further toward agent-driven research, AIR gives us the infrastructure to support both larger models and a faster pace of experimentation. Our experience using AI Runtime has shown us how much reliable, flexible GPU infrastructure matters for research. From large-scale training and governed data access to agent-driven experimentation, AIR lets us spend less time managing infrastructure and more time developing better models. If you're training or fine-tuning your own models, check out the AI Runtime documentation to get started. AI Runtime has also powered our research across areas like faster search , reinforcement learning , and document understanding . item.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
item.abstract: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

item.title: 5 Best Resources to Learn About World Models in 2026
item.abstract: 5 Best Resources to Learn About World Models in 2026 World models could be the next big shift in AI. Learn more right now. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 16, 2026 in Language Models World models are becoming one of the most interesting areas of modern AI research. Instead of simply mapping an input to an output, a world model learns how an environment behaves . It can predict what might happen next, simulate possible outcomes, and help an AI system plan its actions. Although recent systems have brought world models into video generation, robotics, embodied AI, and physical reasoning, many of their fundamental ideas come from reinforcement learning and model-based planning. There is no single resource that takes you from the fundamentals all the way to systems such as Dreamer , Genie , and modern world foundation models, but we do have enough resources to understand how it all works. Here are the five best resources I found for learning about world models in 2026. 1. UC Berkeley CS 285: Deep Reinforcement Learning If you are completely new to world models, I would start here rather than jumping directly into recent world-model papers. UC Berkeley's CS 285: Deep Reinforcement Learning , taught by Sergey Levine, covers the foundations required to understand why world models are useful in the first place. The course covers reinforcement learning, control, and deep learning, and also includes dedicated material on model-based reinforcement learning. The most relevant parts are the lectures on planning, optimal control, learned dynamics, and model-based reinforcement learning. It has lecture recordings, notes, and assignments, so you can study both the mathematics and practical implementations. 2. Stanford CS348K: Introduction to World Models Once you understand some reinforcement learning, Stanford's Introduction to World Models lecture provides a much more direct entry into the topic. The lecture is part of Stanford's Spring 2026 CS348K course and is available online with downloadable PDF slides. It covers visual and spatial computing workloads including generative AI-based world creation, latent world representations, non-pixel-based approaches, and embodied agentic AI. It's not a full course, but it is a good starting point for understanding what world models actually are. 3. World Models by David Ha and Jurgen Schmidhuber This is probably the single most important resource for world models. The original World Models work by David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber popularized a simple but powerful idea: an agent can learn a compressed representation of its environment, learn how that representation evolves, and then train a controller using its internally simulated environment. The architecture consists of three main components. The vision model compresses observations into a smaller latent representation The memory model learns how those latent states change over time The controller uses this learned representation to decide which action to take The most interesting idea is that an agent can sometimes train inside its learned environment rather than interacting with the real environment for every training step. The project website is good for beginners — it includes explanations, diagrams, animations, experiments, and links to the implementation. Even though modern systems such as Dreamer and large video-based world models are more complex, the core intuition is very similar. 4. Stanford World Models and Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Reading List Once you understand the basic idea behind world models, the next step is figuring out what to read. There are now hundreds of papers related to learned dynamics, model-based reinforcement learning, latent environments, generative simulators, and embodied world models. This Stanford reading list provides a much more manageable starting point. It currently highlights ten important papers tracing the progression from early neural world models to modern approaches. The list includes World Models , PlaNet , Dreamer , DreamerV2 , SimPLe , DayDreamer , Genie , and TD-MPC2 . This sequence is useful because you can see how the field evolved. The original World Models showed that an agent could learn a compact internal simulator. PlaNet explored planning directly inside learned latent dynamics. Dreamer shifted toward learning policies using imagined trajectories. Later systems extended similar concepts into robotics and large-scale generative environments. Instead of randomly searching for papers on world models, you can simply work through this reading list one paper at a time. 5. Awesome World Model + Comprehensive World Models Survey Researchers associated with Tsinghua University created the Awesome World Model repository alongside their survey, Understanding World or Predicting Future? A Comprehensive Survey of World Models . The survey was accepted by ACM Computing Surveys , while the repository continuously organizes papers and resources across different branches of world-model research. It covers areas such as: Model-based reinforcement learning Self-supervised learning Large language and multimodal models Video generation and interactive 3D environments Game intelligence and embodied intelligence Autonomous driving and urban intelligence The accompanying survey is especially useful once you have learned the basics, because it explains how all these apparently different research directions fit under the broader world-model umbrella. I would not recommend reading the entire repository from top to bottom. Instead, bookmark it and use it as a reference whenever you want to explore a particular branch of the field. Bonus: World Models Handbook If you prefer learning from a book rather than jumping between lectures and research papers, Michael Brenndoerfer's World Models Handbook is one of the most relevant resources available. It can be read online for free, and a PDF version is also available for purchase. The book is still being completed: the site currently lists 72 planned chapters, with 39 published. It starts with a small end-to-end world model before introducing foundations such as dynamical systems, partial observability, Bayesian filtering, system identification, uncertainty, physics, and causality. Later sections move into modern architectures, including recurrent state-space models, transformers, autoregressive token models, diffusion and flow models, predictive embeddings such as JEPA, and multimodal foundation models . It also covers planning approaches and major research lines — Dreamer, MuZero, TD-MPC, Genie, Cosmos, and vision-language-action models. Wrapping Up World models are not one particular neural-network architecture. They lie at the intersection of reinforcement learning, representation learning, planning, video generation, robotics, control, and embodied AI , which makes them difficult to learn by simply opening the newest paper. A better strategy is to work backward from the fundamentals. First understand how an agent can learn and plan with a model of its environment. Then study the original neural world models architecture. After that, explore how newer research extends the same idea to latent representations, large-scale simulators, video prediction, robotics, and physical AI. Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields. <= Previous post

item.title: Geospatial queries are up to 38X faster with Lakehouse//RT
item.abstract: Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on Lakehouse//RT and they're up to 38X faster than traditional cloud data warehouses. Earlier this year, we brought Spatial SQL to General Availability on Databricks: this included support for the GEOMETRY data type, 100+ spatial functions, high-performance spatial joins, AI/BI maps, Delta Sharing. The GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY data types are part of the open lakehouse, available in Apache Spark, and supported in the same underlying parquet files used by Delta and Iceberg v3. Customers across insurance, agriculture, energy, telecom, retail, logistics and more have adopted it to consolidate geospatial workloads onto a single governed platform. Organizations with both spatial OLAP workloads and real-time location-based applications want great performance and high concurrency. Many of these organizations still rely on traditional data warehouses and build out specialized architectures for spatial applications, sometimes managing a separate stack centered on PostGIS for every use case just to meet latency requirements. Separate stacks lead to more copies of data, more synchronization pipelines, and more governance overhead. Databricks now supports 4-pillars for geospatial workloads: Lakehouse for long-running spatial OLAP workloads, Lakebase for spatial OLTP, apps, and agents, Databricks Apps for purpose-built experiences, and now the Lakehouse//RT warehouse for real-time analytics. This blog covers what Lakehouse//RT delivers for spatial workloads, driving up to 38X performance improvement under high concurrency. We benchmarked Lakehouse//RT against a traditional cloud data warehouse across a suite of spatial queries using SpatialBench . By comparison, Lakehouse//RT delivers 3X faster on average, and up to 20X faster across the tested queries. Under heavy load, the performance differences are even more significant. At 50 concurrent users, Lakehouse//RT delivers up to 38X on the queries where the traditional warehouse could keep up. item.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
item.abstract: Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed. And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.
